reaction-types-s1.title: Five reactions
reaction-types-s1.text: A student lists five reactions seen in lab.

reaction-types-s2.title: Burning an unknown hydrocarbon
reaction-types-s2.text: A 0.8617 g sample of a liquid hydrocarbon is burned completely in excess oxygen. The carbon dioxide and water produced are trapped and weighed. Molar masses: CO₂ 44.01 g/mol; H₂O 18.02 g/mol; C 12.01 g/mol; H 1.008 g/mol.

reaction-types-s3.title: Magnesium in hydrochloric acid
reaction-types-s3.html: Key: green Mg, magnesium atom (in the strip) or Mg²⁺ ion (labeled 2+); small white H with +, H⁺ ion; green Cl with −, chloride ion; two joined white H, H₂ molecule. Water molecules are not drawn.

items.q: Which reaction is a precipitation reaction?
options: Reaction 1
Reaction 2
Reaction 3
Reaction 5

why.correct: In reaction 1 two solutions are mixed and an insoluble solid, PbCl₂(s), forms from ions that were dissolved.
options: Right: two solutions give an insoluble solid.
Reaction 2 makes a gas from a metal and acid; no solid forms from the solutions.
Reaction 3 makes water and a soluble salt; every product stays dissolved or is liquid water.
Reaction 5 is one substance breaking into two; no solid forms.

items.q: In which reactions are electrons transferred? Select all that apply. (Hint: look for an element that is uncombined on one side and part of a compound on the other.)
options: Reaction 1
Reaction 2
Reaction 3
Reaction 5

why.correct: Reaction 2: Mg metal becomes Mg²⁺ and H⁺ becomes H₂. Reaction 5: oxygen in H₂O₂ ends up partly as O₂. In reactions 1 and 3, every ion keeps its charge; ions change partners or an H⁺ moves. (Reaction 4, a combustion, also transfers electrons.)
options: In reaction 1 the ions Pb²⁺, NO₃⁻, Na⁺ and Cl⁻ keep their charges; they only change partners, so no electrons move.
Right: neutral Mg atoms become Mg²⁺ ions and H⁺ ions become neutral H₂.
In reaction 3 an H⁺ moves from HNO₃ to OH⁻; no element changes from uncombined to combined, so no electrons move.
Right: some oxygen leaves the compound as the element O₂.

items.q: Which is the net ionic equation for reaction 3?
options: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l)
K⁺(aq) + NO₃⁻(aq) → KNO₃(aq)
HNO₃(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → NO₃⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) + K⁺(aq)
H⁺(aq) + KOH(aq) → K⁺(aq) + H₂O(l)

why.correct: HNO₃ and KOH are fully ionized in water, and K⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectators. What changes is an H⁺ joining an OH⁻ to make water: the acid-base reaction in its simplest form.
options: Right: only H⁺ and OH⁻ change.
KNO₃(aq) is just the spectator ions dissolved; nothing changes there.
Unbalanced (K⁺ appears from nowhere) and it keeps a spectator.
KOH is a soluble ionic compound, so it is written as K⁺ and OH⁻, and K⁺ is a spectator.

items.q: Reaction 5 is a decomposition. Which other reaction in the table can also be described as one element replacing another in a compound?
options: Reaction 2, where magnesium takes the place of hydrogen
Reaction 1, where lead takes the place of sodium
Reaction 3, where potassium takes the place of hydrogen
Reaction 4, where oxygen takes the place of carbon

why.correct: In reaction 2, the element magnesium ends up in the compound (MgCl₂) and the element hydrogen is set free as H₂: a single replacement. Reactions 1 and 3 swap partners between two compounds (double replacement).
options: Right: an element (Mg) replaces another element (H) in a compound.
Reaction 1 swaps partners between two compounds; no free element takes part.
Reaction 3 swaps partners between two compounds; no element is uncombined on either side.
Reaction 4 is a combustion; carbon is not set free as an element.

items.q: How many moles of hydrogen atoms were in the sample?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the moles of H₂O. Each water molecule holds two H atoms, so double it.
Value: you divided the mass of water by the molar mass of hydrogen. Convert the water to moles of H₂O first, then use 2 mol H per mol H₂O.

why.correct: 1.261 g H₂O × (1 mol H₂O / 18.02 g) × (2 mol H / 1 mol H₂O) = 0.1400 mol H. All the hydrogen in the water came from the hydrocarbon.

items.q: The sample held 0.06001 mol of carbon atoms. What is the empirical formula of the hydrocarbon?
options: C₃H₇
CH₂
C₆H₇
C₃H₈

why.correct: Ratio H : C = 0.1400 ÷ 0.06001 = 2.333, which is 7/3. So the smallest whole-number ratio is C₃H₇ (multiply 1 : 2.333 by 3).
options: Rounds 2.333 down to 2; a ratio this far from a whole number has to be multiplied, not rounded.
Uses moles of water (0.0700) instead of moles of H atoms, so the hydrogen count is halved.
C₃H₈ would need H : C = 2.667, which the data do not give.

items.q: Use the moles of C (0.06001 mol) and of H to find the total mass of carbon and hydrogen in the products. (This checks that the compound contains no oxygen.)

mistakes.why: Value: you added the product masses. Those include oxygen from the air; count only the carbon and hydrogen.

why.correct: 0.06001 mol × 12.01 g/mol = 0.7207 g C; 0.1400 mol × 1.008 g/mol = 0.1411 g H. Total 0.8618 g, which matches the 0.8617 g sample within rounding, so all the mass is C and H.

items.q: The molar mass of the hydrocarbon is found to be about 86 g/mol. Which balanced equation describes its combustion?
options: 2C₆H₁₄ + 19O₂ → 12CO₂ + 14H₂O
C₃H₇ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O
C₆H₁₄ + 19O₂ → 6CO₂ + 7H₂O
2C₆H₁₄ + 13O₂ → 12CO + 14H₂O

why.correct: C₃H₇ has a formula mass of about 43 g/mol, so the molecule is twice that: C₆H₁₄. 2C₆H₁₄ gives 12 CO₂ and 14 H₂O, which hold 24 + 14 = 38 O, so 19 O₂.
options: Right: the molecular formula is C₆H₁₄ and every atom balances.
Uses the empirical formula as if it were the molecule, and the H and O counts do not balance.
Not balanced: 12 C and 28 H on the left but 6 C and 14 H on the right.
Gives carbon monoxide, which forms only when oxygen is short; with excess oxygen the product is CO₂.

items.q: Which net ionic equation matches the diagram?
options: Mg(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + H₂(g)
Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)
Mg(s) + H⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + H(g)
Mg²⁺(aq) + 2Cl⁻(aq) → MgCl₂(s)

why.correct: Two Mg atoms and four H⁺ ions were used; two Mg²⁺ ions and two H₂ molecules formed. That is a 1 : 2 : 1 : 1 ratio. Cl⁻ is unchanged (4 before, 4 after), so it is a spectator.
options: Right: atoms and charge balance (+2 each side) and Cl⁻ is left out.
This is the molecular equation; it keeps the spectator chloride ions.
Unbalanced in atoms and charge, and hydrogen forms H₂ molecules, not single atoms.
No solid MgCl₂ forms; the Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions stay dissolved in the After box.

items.q: Which reactant was limiting in this mixture?
options: H⁺, because none is left while some magnesium remains
Mg, because there were fewer Mg atoms than H⁺ ions
Cl⁻, because it does not appear in the equation
Mg, because one atom remains in the strip

why.correct: H⁺ ran out (4 before, 0 after). One Mg atom is left, so magnesium was in excess.
options: Right: the reactant used up is H⁺.
Fewer particles does not mean limiting: each Mg needs two H⁺, and H⁺ ran out first.
A spectator ion is not a reactant, so it cannot be limiting.
A reactant that is left over is in excess, not limiting.

items.q: How many electrons were transferred from magnesium to hydrogen in the change shown?

mistakes.why: Value: two Mg atoms reacted, but each lost two electrons to become Mg²⁺: 2 × 2 = 4.
Value: only two of the three Mg atoms reacted; the third is still in the strip.

why.correct: Two Mg atoms each lost two electrons (Mg → Mg²⁺): 4 electrons. Four H⁺ ions each gained one electron to form two H₂: 4 electrons. Electrons lost equal electrons gained.

items.q: Which descriptions fit the reaction in the diagram? Select all that apply.
options: Single replacement
Electron transfer
Precipitation
Combustion

why.correct: Magnesium replaces hydrogen (single replacement), and electrons pass from Mg atoms to H⁺ ions. No solid forms from solution and nothing burns in oxygen.
options: Right: the element Mg replaces hydrogen, which is set free as H₂.
Right: neutral Mg becomes Mg²⁺ and H⁺ becomes neutral H₂.
No insoluble solid forms; magnesium dissolves rather than precipitates.
Combustion is a reaction with O₂; there is no oxygen gas here.

items.q: Butane, C₄H₁₀, burns completely in excess oxygen. In the balanced equation with the smallest whole numbers, what is the coefficient of O₂?

why.correct: 2C₄H₁₀ + 13O₂ → 8CO₂ + 10H₂O. The right side has 16 + 10 = 26 O atoms, so 13 O₂. Doubling the butane avoids the fraction 13/2.
options: Right: 2C₄H₁₀ + 13O₂ → 8CO₂ + 10H₂O.
Balances 1 C₄H₁₀ but leaves a fraction; equations use whole numbers, so double everything.
Counts only the oxygen in CO₂ for one butane (4 CO₂ = 8 O) and adds one; the water needs oxygen too.
That is the number of O atoms, not O₂ molecules.

items.q: A gas furnace with a blocked air vent produces a toxic gas. Which equation best explains this?
options: 2CH₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO + 4H₂O
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
CH₄ → C + 2H₂
2CH₄ + O₂ → 2CH₃OH

why.correct: With too little oxygen, carbon ends up as carbon monoxide instead of carbon dioxide: incomplete combustion. CO is colorless, odorless and toxic.
options: Right: incomplete combustion, with too little O₂, makes CO.
This is complete combustion, which needs plenty of oxygen; its products are not the toxic gas.
Methane does not simply break apart in a furnace flame without oxygen being involved.
Making methanol needs special conditions and is not what happens in a furnace.

items.q: Solutions of K₂CO₃ and CaCl₂ are mixed. Calcium carbonate is insoluble; potassium chloride is soluble. Which statement is correct?
options: A precipitate forms: Ca²⁺(aq) + CO₃²⁻(aq) → CaCO₃(s)
No reaction occurs, because both starting compounds are soluble
A precipitate of KCl forms, because it is the other product
A gas forms, because carbonate releases CO₂ in water

why.correct: The new combination Ca²⁺ with CO₃²⁻ is insoluble, so it precipitates. K⁺ and Cl⁻ stay dissolved as spectators.
options: Right: the insoluble combination precipitates.
Soluble starting compounds can still make an insoluble product when their ions meet new partners.
Potassium chloride is soluble, so its ions stay dissolved.
Carbonate gives off CO₂ when an acid is added, not in plain water with calcium ions.

items.q: Which are decomposition reactions? Select all that apply.
options: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g)
2KClO₃(s) → 2KCl(s) + 3O₂(g)
2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s)
Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s)

why.correct: A decomposition starts with one substance and gives two or more. Sodium plus chlorine is a synthesis; zinc in copper(II) sulfate is a single replacement.
options: Right: one compound gives two products.
Right: one compound gives two products.
Two elements combine into one compound: a synthesis, the reverse of decomposition.
Zinc replaces copper in the compound: a single replacement.
